mcqs.question: How does a hardware atomic instruction achieve indivisibility, compared to a mutex?
options: The CPU itself guarantees it for that instruction, with no OS or scheduler coordination needed
It relies on the OS scheduler pausing every other thread in the system
It requires the programmer to manually disable interrupts
It works identically to a mutex, just with a different name
mcqs.explanation: A hardware atomic instruction is indivisible at the CPU level (via bus locking or cache-coherence protocols), with no scheduler or OS involvement — unlike a mutex, which coordinates access to a region of code by making other threads wait. It doesn't pause the whole system or require manual interrupt handling, and it is a fundamentally different mechanism from a lock.

mcqs.question: In the CAS-based counter increment loop, what happens when atomic_compare_exchange_weak fails?
options: The program crashes, since CAS failure is treated as a fatal error
The thread blocks until the lock is available
old_val is refreshed with the current value and the read-compute-CAS sequence retries
The increment is silently skipped and the loop exits
mcqs.explanation: A CAS failure just means another thread updated the value first; the call refreshes old_val to the actual current value and the loop retries with fresh data — no blocking, no crash, and no skipped increment. This retry-on-failure behavior is the defining trait of lock-free code, as opposed to blocking on contention.

mcqs.question: Why can't a plain compare-and-swap detect the ABA problem?
options: CAS only checks whether the current value matches the expected value, and can't tell that value changed and changed back in between
CAS operations are not actually atomic on most hardware
ABA only happens with floating-point values, which CAS doesn't support
CAS always fails when any other thread has touched the location, regardless of the final value
mcqs.explanation: CAS's contract is purely value-based: if the location currently equals the expected value, succeed. It has no way to know the value took a detour through something else in between, which is exactly the ABA scenario. CAS instructions are genuinely atomic in hardware, ABA isn't restricted to floats, and CAS succeeds (not always fails) whenever the value matches, regardless of intermediate history.

mcqs.question: Thread A writes data = 42, then atomically sets ready = true. Thread B spins until ready == true, then reads data, but sometimes still sees the old value. What is the most likely cause?
options: The atomic store to ready is not actually atomic on this hardware
This can never actually happen if ready is declared atomic, so the described bug is impossible
Thread B is reading data before calling any atomic operation at all, which is always undefined
Insufficient memory ordering guarantees allowed the writes to data and ready to become visible to thread B out of program order
mcqs.explanation: Atomicity of the ready flag alone doesn't guarantee ordering between the writes to different variables (data and ready) becomes visible in program order to another thread — that requires explicit memory ordering (release/acquire) to establish a happens-before relationship. The store to ready being atomic is not in question; the bug is a real, well-known reordering hazard, not an impossibility.

mcqs.question: A team decides to replace all their mutexes with hand-rolled CAS loops because lock-free code 'avoids deadlock.' What is the biggest risk in this decision?
options: Lock-free code trades deadlock/priority-inversion bugs for a different, often harder-to-find set like ABA and memory-ordering violations
CAS loops are always slower than mutexes in every scenario
Lock-free code cannot be used with more than two threads
There is no real risk — lock-free code is strictly safer than lock-based code
mcqs.explanation: Avoiding deadlock doesn't mean avoiding bugs — lock-free code introduces its own hard-to-find failure modes (ABA, memory-ordering violations, manual-memory-reclamation bugs) that are often harder to reproduce and debug than a deadlock. It isn't universally slower, isn't limited to two threads, and is not strictly safer overall — it's a different risk profile, not a free upgrade.

mcqs.question: You suspect a lock-free data structure has an ABA-related bug causing rare, unreproducible corruption. What is the most effective way to surface it for debugging?
options: Add print statements throughout the code, since printing won't affect timing
Run the code under ThreadSanitizer with a stress test that maximizes contention, and use a debug allocator that poisons freed memory to turn silent corruption into an immediate crash
Rewrite the entire application to be single-threaded temporarily
Increase the thread priority of the affected threads
mcqs.explanation: ThreadSanitizer tracks happens-before relationships across atomics and can catch many of these bugs, and a debug allocator that poisons freed memory converts a subtle use-after-reuse bug into a loud, immediate crash that's actually debuggable. Print statements do change timing and can hide the bug (a Heisenbug), a single-threaded rewrite defeats the purpose of testing a concurrency bug, and thread priority is unrelated to correctness.
